# The Skaeling Coast

*Pages PDF 48-57*

## **The Skaeling Coast Settlements of the Skaeling Norse Skilled Sailors and Feared Raiders**
The Skaeling Coast is a ragged coastline of mighty cliffs, countless deep, twisting fjords, and innumerable rocky islands. Fish, orca, and whales fill the sea, along with sharks and far more terrible marine monstrosities. 

Although cold and often bleak, the land is not sterile, its more sheltered valleys and southern slopes covered with forests of fir and pine. 

Thickly-furred animals, from squirrels and goats to wolves and bears, live among the trees and in hidden caves. Unnatural reptiles live here too, from rock lizards, wyverns, and basilisks, to true dragons — thankfully mostly asleep. 

The region is dominated by the Skaelings, who live, fight, and survive in the cold lands and waters. Their longships are common here, and even the crews of fishing vessels are capable warriors. Their attitude to outsiders is variable to say the least, making travel to and exploration of the Coast an uncertain, nerve-wracking experience. 

Many mysteries lie hidden here. Besides the known Norse Dwarf holds, there are said to be secret ones tunnelled into the cliffs, inhabited by reclusive clans who avoid their brethren for their own reasons. Towers seen from the sea blink with bizarrely coloured lights, hinting at the magic of Chaos sorcerers. Strangely carved monoliths record forgotten histories and promise gifts from dark powers. 

Despite the many dangers, the Skaeling Coast lures many from the Old World and beyond. The Skaeling tribes have few creative industries beyond the forging of weapons and armour, leatherworking, and textiles. 

This provides Old World merchants with great opportunities to trade their luxuries for rare timbers, gold from Norscan mountains, and high-quality weapons. The port of Kirkjugarður Langskipa is arguably the safest trading destination, but it is not for the faint-hearted. Alongside the merchants are explorers, scholars, and warriors, seeking adventure, secrets, and glory. 

## **Norse Raiders**
Without question, the Norse are a preeminent sea-faring nation. Their longships are not as beautiful as Elven Hawkships, not as powerful as the Dwarfs’ Ironclads, and not as high-sided as the vessels of the Empire or Bretonnia. However, they are sleek, fast, and enduring. Probably only the Elves are as experienced and fartravelled on the seas as the Norse. And undoubtedly, there are few sights on the sea more intimidating than the dragon prow of a Norse longship. 

Down the centuries, the northern coast of the Old World has experienced Norse raids time and time again. The Skaelings are responsible for many attacks, but other tribes commonly raid, too. Kislev, Ostland, Nordland, Marienburg, and Bretonnia have all fallen victim to assault over the centuries, although all have pushed back and reclaimed their own lands. However, raiding is so normal for some remote villages that they have come to terms with the raiders and offer tribute (both goods and people) in exchange for being left alone. This is easier than waiting for the local lord to send troops after the raiders have already gone. Imperial authorities have outlawed this practice, although enforcing it is virtually impossible. 

Unfortunately, not all Norse raiders are motivated by practical needs or greed. The Skaelings especially do it for the thrill of battle and to praise Khorne. This makes it harder to appease them through tribute and offerings, and their attacks are bloody and often to the death, unless they can be forced back or impressed by a foe’s tenacity. 

Far more dangerous, however, are the times when a great Chaos Champion arises from any of the tribes. Blessed by the Dark Gods, they frequently call for war. Whether by force of fist or personality, these Champions draw different tribes and monsters together, bringing Chaos and death to all standing in their way. They set sail in great fleets and lay siege to ports, laying waste to the coast. They have attacked Erengrad, sailed as far as Praag, and even travelled down the Reik to attack Altdorf. Even Middenheim has been assaulted. 

They are also great whalers, for whales provide meat, oil, and strong bone, as well as simple challenge. For those cowardly Old World merchants unwilling to brave the cold and dangers of Norsca itself, Norscan traders are willing to meet them halfway, exchanging goods in the middle of the Sea of Claws. Nor is it uncommon for them to peacefully visit the larger ports to trade their wares. They even offer their services as ship-board mercenaries or protective escorts at sea, quite happy to fight against other Norse if an honest deal has been struck. 

The other strand of Norse seafaring is exploration. The Skaelings often explore with a view to raiding new lands, but there are many Norse captains and crews just as interested in discovering new places simply for the risk and adventure of it. The most famous of these is the Bjornling Losteriksson, who discovered Lustria, but others have ventured even further afield, to countless mysterious islands and stranger shores. Some proudly haul back the rotting carcasses of horrible sea monsters. Others tell of whirlpools to other worlds and fields of rusting metal windmills sprouting from the sea. 

## Raiders or Traders?
After a terrible storm, the Characters discover the bodies of several Norsemen washed up on a beach near a settlement where they are staying. Some are still alive, although unconscious. What looks like a variety of trade goods have also washed up. Were these Norsemen traders, or are these goods the ill-gotten gains of merciless piracy? What do the Characters do when the townsfolk decide it’s best to kill the still-breathing Norsemen where they lie? 

## Out on the Ice
On a frozen beach in north-western Norsca, Characters spy the beached ship of Skaeling seal-hunters. It’s an unpleasant business, and kindly Characters might intercede on the seals’ behalf. However, if the Characters take the time to look, these seals have two–inch long poison fangs… and they’re not afraid to use them! 

All Norse tribes, even the Skaelings, sail not only for raiding and war, but for practical reasons. Fish is the staple of the Norse diet, and a longship is as likely casting nets as looking for trouble. 

## **Piracy and the Norse**
The Norse are infamous for raiding and marauding, so it is no surprise that they have a reputation as wanton pirates. Even the more civilized Norse tribes, such as the Bjornlings, are happy to indulge in piracy if the opportunity presents itself, or if circumstances prevent them from making a living from honest trade. 

Even those brave merchants from other Old World nations who are willing to trade with the Norse feel a pang of fear should they spot the silhouette of a longship on the horizon. Longship captains and their crews often bear little loyalty to anyone but themselves, so even a merchant with a history of trading with a particular Norse tribe will not necessarily benefit from their goodwill if he encounters their vessels at sea. 

Yet for many in the Old World the archetypal pirate is not regarded as Norse, but Tilean. This is even the case along the northern shores of the Empire, where the corsairs of the Tilean Sea are a distant threat, and Norse raiders a constant danger. 

## **The Norse and Stromfels**
Those with a little knowledge of Stromfels assume him to be a god of piracy (those who know more would challenge this, stating that he is better understood as a god of predation and the violence of the sea, and that pirates merely fit the theme rather than exemplify it). 

Many assume he is a Norse deity, given his violent nature and his popularity among reavers, but if he was ever a god of the Norse they have apparently abandoned him in favour of darker powers. Unpleasant as Stromfels is, he represents an aspect of the natural world, and is no friend to followers of Chaos. 

Because of the links between the practices of Stromfels and the practices of piracy, the Norse are often shunned by others who live by piracy. 

## **The Norse and Sartosa**
The one place where pirates are assured of a haven (albeit a haven from the laws of kings and burgomeisters, not from each other) is the island of Sartosa. It is found to the south of the Tilean Sea and is governed by a council of pirate captains and their elected representative. Codes and fashions common to professional (for want of a better word) pirates have their origins here, and the island is home to the world’s only overt temple to Stromfels. 

Yet here the story comes full circle, for Sartosa owes much of its culture to waves of colonisation and conquest, and among the varied seaborne raiders who settled here are the Norse, many of whom live among the Sartosans to this day. 

One of the rising stars among the reavers who currently plague the Tilean Sea is the Queen of Tides, a mutant pirate captain with a noted hatred of the Norse. Aboard her vessel, the Swordfysh, she has engaged and sunk many longships, striking without mercy. Yet there are those who say her own origins trace back to the icy fjords of the Bjornling Coast, and that her campaign against the Norse is driven by a desire for vengeful patricide. 

## **The Skaelings**
Although considered one cultural group, mostly following the same customs and rules, Skaeling tribes are many, varied, and scattered across the Skaeling Coast and mountains beyond. If they have no immediate cause to fight outsiders, they easily find cause to fight one another: for territory, tribute, ancient grievance, because Khorne demands it, or simply for the thrill of battle. They are ardent Chaos worshippers, though not as manically bloodthirsty and twisted as the Varg, the Aesling, or the multitudinous Kurgan tribes, against whom they arguably buffer the Old World. They have more in common with the Sarls, although they consider the Sarls’ lesser enthusiasm for blood sacrifice a sign of weakness. Bjornlings are often dismissed as being more traders than warriors, and insufficiently zealous in their appreciation of Khorne. 

## On Tribes
Norse tribes are complicated. While there are Great Tribes like the Sarls, Skaelings, Aeslings, and Bjornlings, as well as Lesser ones, there are also tribes within them. There are kin-tribes, which are extended families. There are tribes named for the settlements, regions, or fortresses they control. A longship’s crew usually considers itself a tribe. Most tribes are connected by tangled webs of kinships, oaths, debts, grievances, alliances, and enmities. Outsiders must be careful who they praise or criticise, for risk of stepping on the wrong strand. 

The Skaelings proclaim themselves a sea-faring people, great shipbuilders, and mighty raiders. The sailors of the northern Old World certainly agree, with a few pejoratives attached. Despite this, the many Skaeling tribes pay allegiance to a place deep inland: Doomkeep. 

There resides the king of the Skaelings, Felman Ingersson, to whom all other Skaeling jarls swear loyalty (even if it’s sometimes begrudged). Why a sea-faring culture should place its capital so far from the sea is a mystery, and with mystery comes speculation and legend. It may be for security — a capital so deep in the mountains is harder to attack. It’s closer to the lands of Chaos, so it could be a symbolic act of devotion. A more mythic claim is that it’s where a great chieftain of the Norsii was laid to rest after battling a strange Forest Spirit named Treeblood. 

Another tale suggests an ancient relic is protected there, one that must stay far from the sea or it will unleash a forgotten terror upon the world. However, it’s also claimed many Skaelings live far away on the coast to avoid constant supervision and control by a king or queen. When asked, Skaelings just shrug, changing the subject. 

The tribe claim that they are something more than human, attributing their origins to a vast Ice Drake that roamed the Troll Country. They tattoo themselves with dragon devices to honour this mythic ancestor. 

The Skaelings also boast their ferocity as warriors and devotion to Chaos. They acknowledge all gods, but especially Kharnath (Khorne), whose symbol adorns their ships, weapons, and bodies. Mutations beneficial in battle or for survival are considered blessings from the gods, those creating weakness curses; both affect social standing. Mutants who are neither strengthened nor weakened are considered merely god-touched, perhaps destined to be seers or vitki. 

Skaelings unashamedly practise human and animal sacrifice, but most believe human sacrifice to Kharnath best takes place naturally within battle, whether in war, raiding, or ritual duels. Humans brought to the altar like animals are considered to be animals: oath-breakers, weaklings, cowards, traitors, and criminals unable to pay wergild. Although bloody, most sacrifices are swift; few Skaelings indulge in ritualised torture of sacrifices, for that is not battle. That said, Skaeling warriors do practise ritual scarification, where much blood flows. Skaelings respect anyone who sheds blood this way for their god, even weak gods; a Shallyan priestess who accepts a dove symbol carved into her shoulder is as respected as a Skaeling who accepts Khorne’s skull. Almost. 

Though disdainful of them for what they see as weak stomachs for sacrifice, the Skaeling consider the Sarl their main rivals in battle, territory, and skill at boatbuilding. The buffer between their two lands is the mutually sacred Bay of Blades and the nearby port, the Altar of the Crimson Harvest. The latter is in Sarl lands, but Skaeling are welcome and their bloodier values respected there. The two tribes tussle for territory, especially inland, but along the coastline, sea or land, bloodshed is limited and conducted with honour and respect. Inevitably, there are many ties of kith and kin, and when threatened by outsiders or mutual threats, they are all Norse together. 

## **The Hall of the Snaegr**
The Snaegr are a Skaeling tribe for whom Khorne-worship is their driving purpose. A former jarl, Urlf, was so ardent and brutal in his devotion that Khorne elevated him to Daemonhood, becoming Urlfdaemonkin. After this, the tribe began worshipping Urlfdaemonkin alongside Khorne, and considered themselves favoured by Khorne above all others. The anniversary of Ulrf ’s ascendance is called the _Moon-time of Urlf_ , and has become a time to travel south, attacking all in their path, even other Skaelings. During Moon-time it is common for Snaegr warriors to be temporarily god-blessed, shapeshifting into creatures mirroring Urlfdaemonkin’s form. One of Urlf ’s descendants, Grydal, is the tribe’s current jarl, and he seeks Urlfdaemonkin’s blessing permanently. 

## Help Us, Please!
Several Snaegr peasants run south, fleeing the wrath of a Snaegr warrior. Encountering the Characters, they beg for protection. Unfortunately, the warrior is bringing friends. The situation is complicated by the fact that those fleeing killed the warrior’s wife, who discovered them stealing. The peasants face brutal death, but the warrior has a legitimate grievance. 

## There Is a Price
The Characters need a Skaeling tribe’s knowledge or aid. Unfortunately, in return they must help fight the Snaegr during Moon-time or seek the return of a respected warrior’s skull from the Snaegr hall. 

The Snaegr are a thorn in the side of many other Skaeling tribes, for they fight for the sake of violence and blood alone, and will not come to terms. They have to be driven back by force or simply endured until the Snaegr deem Moon-time over. The Snaegr blessed with Urlfdaemonkin’s form are an especially dangerous challenge, although their cannibalistic nature sometimes slows them down. 

## **Monolith of Borkhill the Bloody-Handed**
A Chaos Monolith records the deeds of Borkhill, and tells the tale of his hunt for the Giant Maulgrong and discovery of a black pillar containing a Chaos chalice. Drinking deep, Borkhill grew mighty with dark power, helping him defeat his Giant foe. 

## Exalted Snaegr
The black pillar exists: a slim obsidian spire, with a violet sphere of energy crackling at its pinnacle. At its base is a geode-like cavity containing the chalice, filled with a silver liquid, bearing the scent of dreams. 

Snaegr blessed by Urlfdaemonkin gain the following traits: Big, Fury, Hardy, Hungry, and Tusks +7. The blessing lasts only for the Moon-time of Urlf, an uncertain, inherently Chaotic length of time. If Characters encounter the Snaegr, the GM may make a secret Test to see if it is the Moon-time of Urlf. There is a 20% chance of it being the Moon-time in the months of Vorgeheim and Vorhexen, and an 8% chance during the rest of the year. The Moon-time of Urlf lasts d10 days, and then will not occur again until the following year. 

Drinking from the cup fulfils the drinker’s foremost need by transforming them. In Borkhill’s case, he needed the might to defeat a Giant; so, he became giant-like, bigger, and stronger. Thus, any drinker becomes, in some manner, more like their own immediate challenge in order to overcome it. 

The hall of the Snaegr is carved deep into a mountainside, and contains many rooms, passages, and battle-trophies. Here Jarl Grydal and his warriors reside, practising bloody rites. Skulls of beasts and men fill niches around the entrance. On the cleared slopes below are the wooden homes of down-trodden Snaegr peasants and thralls who ensure the basic needs of the warriors are met. The road to the hall zig-zags up through thick forest and small level areas cleared for limited cultivation. 

If a drinker simply needs to get through the mountains, her body transforms into cold stone, with its strength and hardiness, though also becomes slower of foot. If another hunts a stag, his legs become deer-like, enduring and fleet. The drinker who, more than any immediate quest, seeks their true love, becomes very similar (though not identical) to the person they seek, whoever that might be. The effects last only as long as the need. Hopefully. 

Evidence of Khorne worship is all about: gory shrines, skull-laden branches, and the stench of rancid blood. 

## **Kirkjugarður Langskipa**
Kirkjugarður Langskipa is an open port, routinely receiving ships from many nations and cultures from around the Sea of Claws. It’s perhaps a greater melting pot than almost anywhere else, even Marienburg. After all, Marienburg doesn’t tolerate mutants, Orcs, or human sacrifice — at least not openly. However, tolerance is not acceptance, and some outsiders are more resented than others, making it dangerous for non-Norse to venture beyond the docks. Strength and skill-at-arms, however, are widely respected, though they do encourage challenges from those who wish to test their own. Even the most formidible fighter must beware which streets they walk. 

The outstanding feature of the port is its buildings, which are overwhelmingly built from the hulls of ships shattered in battle. Many are Norse longships, but there are houses and public buildings constructed from the upturned hulls of ships of all nations. Figureheads are used as decoration and statuary, though all are overlooked by a massive brass monolith festooned with the bones of the vanquished. Faded, paint-peeled ships’ badges are split for window-shutters. Masts and sidearms are used as supporting pillars, wharf-posts, and places to nail sacrifices to Kharnath. The architecture is an intimidating reminder of Skaeling naval strength. Many residents are raiders, and other raiders visit to resupply and boast. 

The docks are busy and routinely salted and gritted to prevent slippery ice; salt-stained boots and leggings are to be expected. There are smokehouses and warehouses full of salted and smoked fish, giving the place a distinctive smell. Secure buildings hold slaves before sale, although it is not a major slave port. There are taverns for sailors, inns for travellers and merchants, and shops for everyone. Shipyards loudly hammer and saw. Sturdy wagons work their way inland through streets cleared of snow by thralls, following routes into the mountains. 

The town is ruled by Öskra Örninn and his wife Signe. Öskra’s family have ruled the town for many generations, and it is expected his daughter, Gertrud, will succeed him, as she is already god-blessed with a bony spine protruding from her forearm. Öskra is a powerful man and experienced raider. However, he recognises his town’s prosperity and survival means balancing openness to outsiders with bloodshed against aggressors and troublemakers. 

## **Velkominn Allt**
Velkominn Allt is a sailors’ inn where crew of all species, faiths, tribes, and natures are accepted. The landlord, Harwullf Ironcast, and his family tolerate no bigotry and step on any hint of it before trouble starts. The prices are fair, the beds clean, and the food good. Non-sailors are welcome to eat and drink, but beds are usually for captains and merchants. Those seeking news, information, and interesting, useful people can find much here. 

## Small Minds
A charismatic agitator stirs trouble, decrying the Velkominn Allt’s acceptance of outsiders. Initially laughable, over a few weeks her following swells. Those entering the inn are initially mocked, then stones get thrown. Soon there are incidents of night-time beatings. Harwulf asks the Characters to discreetly kill the agitator, before a full-scale riot engulfs the docks. 

## Drunken Sailor
Harwulf slips the Characters a few pfennigs to see a drunken captain, an old friend, safely back to his ship. On the way, they are jumped by brigands. The captain has something (a secret, a map?) someone powerful wants. 

## **Skarlati Dreki**
Skarlati Dreki is the red-lacquered prow of a longship, part of a fleet assembled decades ago to challenge a Dark Elf Black Ark. The conflict was so terrible that every ship, even the Ark, was sunk. Save for a dozen hardy survivors clinging to it, this dragon prow was all that remained, and was preserved as a monument to Norscan fearlessness. 

## Return to Sea
A handful of old men and women, the last of those rescued after the Great Battle, are looking for a crew to take them to its site. This seems easy enough, but they also want to steal Skarlati Dreki, believing it should join its ship. They may also have sinister motives. 

## Dreki Speaks!
A loud draconic voice emanating from the monument could call for anything: war with the Dark Elves, blood sacrifice (any Elf suffices), material tribute (which vanishes overnight), reaffixing to a longship with a crew. Is this a ventriloquist’s ploy? A wizard’s magic? Or has a dark spirit awakened within it? 

## **Temple of Mermedus**
On the port’s outskirts is a beach avoided by anyone without good reason to visit. This lonesome patch of sand and pebbles stinks of the rot of the sea and is smothered with clumps of dark seaweed alive with sand fleas. Abutted against a steep cliff-face lies a rotting hull, covered in sea moss, barnacles, and stranger encrustations. This is the local temple to Mermedus. 

The Skaeling believe this Daemonic entity dwells beneath the Sea of Claws. They depict him as a pale, bloated figure, covered in bulging eyes. He is said to wander about on the ocean floor, causing stormy waters to capsize ships and drown sailors. To appease this vile god, the Skaeling make Human and animal sacrifices, casting the weighted bodies down to distract the god from their voyage. 

More sinister than the place itself is the temple’s priest and guardian, Gröftur Fiskauga. Gröftur is a disturbing character, with large staring eyes uncomfortably reminiscent of a dead fish. Although he wears foulsmelling robes, where the backs of his hands and neck are exposed, one can see the short, white, sea-urchin spines that cover the dorsal half of his body. Although unpleasant, he can use his voice well, becoming a powerful orator, suddenly shifting pitch from high to low, volume from loud to quiet, changing like the moods of the sea. 

Gröftur is a mercurial figure. Though consistently foulsmelling and unnerving, he flits from good humour to foul temper. He offers honest praise as often as contemptuous sarcasm. It’s entirely possible for Characters to consistently see just one side of him, only to be shocked one day when he’s completely the opposite. Most find him hard to deal with, so he is avoided unless people are desperate for blessing or guidance. However, he never rejects anyone or ever tells them to go away. That’s one sure thing about Mermedus: it happily accepts anything or anyone into its briny embrace. 

## A Fishy Judgement
Slightly outnumbered by aggressive local Skaelings, the Characters are given the choice of fighting to the death or submitting themselves to Gröftur Fiskauga’s judgement. Gröftur asks them to bind themselves to Mermedus’s will for one season; it’s that or fight. 

## The Blue Conch
Gröftur requires a blue conch to make a sacred horn. He suggests the Characters try Hornborg’s shop in Skjold; Hornburg directs them to the shallow waters around a distant island. After a challenging journey and return, Gröftur gives them each three, knotted strings; untying a knot triggers a Blessing (choice of Breath, Fortune, or Hardiness). 

## **Vargr Lodge**
The Skaelings are a ferocious tribe, openly venerating Kharnath, the incarnation of Khorne best known to their people. For many Skaelings, life is a constant struggle between the bloody urge for violence and the stability needed for survival. When the shadow of Chaos grows they sail forth to raid and slaughter. When it recedes, the Skaelings become more settled, although there is a nagging sense that Kharnath is displeased. 

Some cannot make the adjustment. The Vargr Lodge is a primitive wooden shelter on the forest edge north _ulfwerener_ of Kirkjugarður Langskipa. This is where the (‘Skin Wolves’) and the wildest berserkers dwell, those who struggle to integrate in quieter times. They live like a pack of animals, fighting each other, hunting by night, and collapsing around the fire pit to sleep during the day. 

Despite their ferality, the inhabitants of the Vargr Lodge are melancholy during their lucid hours. They’re shunned by the Skaelings in the town as too disruptive to tolerate outside of battle, although family members occasionally brave the Lodge to leave food or speak with relatives. Only when their savagery is needed do their neighbours visit, to goad them into action. Those who can control themselves for some time may find work as wilderness guides or bodyguards for a jarl, but even then they are treated with caution. 

## Ragnulf’s Hoard
Ragnulf was once a proud huscarl in the jarl’s retinue, always at the forefront in battle. He amassed a fortune in silver and amber, but he did not trust other Skaelings and kept his hoard hidden. One day in a skirmish with the Sarls, he succumbed to bloodlust, lost control, and became a near mindless berserker. 

Now Ragnulf lives in the Vargr Lodge, a tragic, hollow shadow of his former self. Memories of his former life occasionally drift to the surface — which is an opportunity, because everyone in the jarl’s hall wants to know where he hid his hoard. 

## **Olg Blóðsalt**
To other Norse, especially Skaelings, Olg Blóðsalt is a god-blessed champion. At the age of 19 he has already risen to the rank of ship’s captain. To those unfamiliar with the ways of the Norse he appears sinister, but apparently less formidable than the straight-backed and muscular frames of those under his command. His god-blessing, the Brine Drinker mutation, means that his body is stocky and puffy, encrusted with wet, sticky salt. His taut pale skin and knotted red hair age his appearance considerably. In his rusted armour, with his rusted weapons, only the perceptive, and those who have seen him in battle, understand he is a ferocious warrior and raider. 

Olg’s ferocity is born of bitterness and resentment of this supposed blessing. He did not choose this gift; it was imposed upon him. Being seen as powerful is meaningless if one is also seen as old and ugly, especially for one in his prime. He is envious of the loved and the handsome, but despite his anger knows they are no more responsible for their condition than he is his own.

A few have offered lies as solutions to delay death or thralldom; when they failed, their fates were even more terrible. 

## Chaos Mutation: Brine Drinker
Someone with this mutation can drink salt water without harm. In addition to its survival advantage at sea, it allows the mutant to spew a torrent of corrosive, stinging, salty vomit. This is a Vomit attack, except that instead of taking damage the target must pass a **Difficult (–10) Endurance** Test or gain one _Blinded_ Condition, and any metal armour they are wearing has its Armour Rating halved (round up), as the metal immediately begins to rust. The mutant’s skin is permanently covered with a salty wet crust, and they must drink a pint of briny sea water (not just water with salt added) every day, otherwise they gain a _Fatigued_ Condition. 

## **Norse Characters**
If you wish to generate a Character from Norsca these rules can be used rather than the rules for Characters from the Reikland on page 36 of the **WFRP Core Rulebook** . It is up to players and GMs to think about how a Norse Character might impact a typical party of adventurers. Even the more civilised Norse Characters have been brought up in a society that legitimises a form of respect for the gods of Chaos and inculcates their young in the value of fostering personal resilience and regarding those who don’t as weak fools. 

Starting characters may choose 3 Skills to gain 5 Advances each, and 3 Skills to gain 3 Advances each. If a Talent listing presents a choice, you select one Talent from the choices given. Any Random Talents are determined by the Random Talent table ( **WFRP** , page 36). If you roll a Talent you already have, you may reroll. Norse characters speak Norse as a first language. 

## **Humans (Bjornling Norse)**
**Skills:** Consume Alcohol, Evaluate, Gossip, Haggle, Language (Reikspiel), Language (Wastelander), Lore (Norsca), Melee (Basic), Row, Sail, Swim, Trade (Any) 

**Talents:** Fisherman _or_ War Leader, Resistance (Chaos), Sea Legs _or_ Warrior Born, 2 Random Talents 

## **Humans (Sarl Norse)**
**Skills:** Animal Care, Consume Alcohol, Gossip, Language (Reikspiel), Language (Gospodarinyi), Lore (Norsca), Melee (Basic), Ride, Row, Sail, Swim, Trade (choose one) 

**Talents:** Crack the Whip _or_ Old Salt, Resistance (Chaos), Roughrider _or_ Sea Legs, 2 Random Talents 

## New Creature Trait: the Mark of Khorne
Khorne has marked this creature with a physical brand, proclaiming it sworn to his cause. The creature benefits from the _Frenzy_ Talent. This creature gains the Etiquette (Followers of Khorne) Talent and is subject to Animosity towards overt followers of Slaanesh. The creature is also subject to Animosity by followers of Slaanesh, so long as the Mark of Khorne is visible. The Character may never use the Language (Magick) or Channelling skills unless it is to dispel a spell. 

Additonally they may purchase the following Talents as if they were Career Advances for the normal XP costs: Berserk Charge, Combat Aware, Combat Reflexes, Furious Assault, Implacable, Magic Resistance, Resistance (Magic), Resolute, Strike Mighty Blow, Warrior Born.

## **Human (Skaeling Norse)**
**Skills:** Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Language (Reikspiel), Language (Wastelander), Lore (Khorne), Melee (Basic), Melee (Two-Handed), Row, Sail, Swim 

**Talents:** Beneath Notice _or_ Resolute, Berserk Charge _or_ Flee!, Resistance (Chaos), 2 Random Talents 

**Surnames:** Norse Humans often use the same system for surnames that is common among Dwarfs, a shared tradition whose heritage is traced back to the bonds of trade Norse Humans and Norse Dwarfs shared in ages past. This system is detailed on page 38 of the **WFRP Core Rulebook** , though Norse nicknames do not use Khazalid and centre on personal prowess, intimidating boasts, or claims to kinship with daemons or monsters. 

A Skaeling Character who generates the _Pure Soul_ Talent as a Random Talent may take the _Mark of Khorne_ instead. 

## **Norse Careers**
Norse Characters may generate starting careers using the table below. Whilst Norse careers are limited in scope, they count as Humans for the purpose of taking on new careers, so whilst a Norse Character may not start their career as a wizard, they do have the potential to become a Wizard if the opportunity to do so presents itself. 

GMs and players should consider what Norse society is like when creating Characters. An Artisan, for example, may well be a boatbuilder or blacksmith, but would not manage a printing press.

## Advice on Norse Skills, Talents, and Trappings
Norse society is very different to that of the rest of the Old World, isolated both geographically and culturally from the south. There are a great many trades, technologies, and trappings that are familiar to the folk of the Empire and Kislev that are unknown, or shunned, by the Norse. Certain careers are also included to cover Norse careers with many roles (a Skald, for example, may encompass what it is to be an Agitator, Scholar, and Entertainer; a Vitki might be a Nun, Mystic, and/or Witch). 

Wherever a Career suggests a Character acquire the Skills, Talents and Trappings to use Ranged (Blackpowder, Engineering, or Crossbow), a Norse Character need only learn to master Ranged (Throwing) instead. Similarly, Melee (Fencing) should be substituted for Melee (Two-Handed). Plate Armour is rare in Norsca, so Chainmail will suffice if armour is needed as a trapping. GMs and players should consider any Skill, Talent, or Trapping that does not suit the lifestyle or aesthetic of the Norse as an option, or replace them with suitable alternatives. 

A Norse Character who starts a new life in another part of the world may ignore such restrictions.
